seo.title: UTM Parameters in Google Analytics: A Guide
seo.meta_description: How to add UTM parameters to links so Google Analytics shows which emails, social posts and Business Profile links bring Orange County customers.

h1: UTM Parameters in Google Analytics: Track Every Campaign Link
answer: UTM parameters are tags you add to the end of a link, such as utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign, so Google Analytics can show which email, social post or ad brought each visitor. Google says you should always use those three, and the values appear in the Traffic acquisition report. Anaheim and Orange County businesses can use them to measure every campaign link.
key_takeaways: Always use utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign.
Values show in the Traffic acquisition report.
Auto-tagging handles Google Ads; UTMs handle the rest.

sections.heading: What UTM parameters do
sections.body_html: Google's help page explains that adding UTM campaign parameters to the links you use in referral links and campaigns lets you see which campaigns refer traffic. When someone clicks a tagged link, the values are sent to Analytics and appear in the Traffic acquisition report.

sections.heading: The parameters
sections.body_html:
ParameterWhat it identifiesExample
utm_sourceThe referrernewsletter, facebook
utm_mediumThe marketing mediumemail, cpc, social
utm_campaignThe campaign or promotionspring_sale
utm_contentWhich creative or linkheader_button
utm_termPaid keywordroof repair
utm_idCampaign IDan internal ID

Source: Google Analytics Help.

sections.heading: Always use the core three
sections.body_html: Google says that when you add parameters to a URL, you should always use utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign. Its example for a summer email: utm_source=summer-mailer, utm_medium=email and utm_campaign=summer-sale.

sections.heading: Consistency matters
sections.body_html: Google's best practices say to use one unique source per platform, one medium per channel and one name per campaign. It stresses that values are case-sensitive, so Meta and meta are treated as different values, and recommends lowercase as a standard.

sections.heading: Use a URL builder
sections.body_html: Google provides URL builders that add the parameters for you, which reduces typos. Many ad platforms also support dynamic parameters that fill in values automatically.

sections.heading: Where to see the data
sections.body_html: Tagged visits appear in the Traffic acquisition report under Session source, Session medium and Session campaign. Google notes UTM parameters are omitted from the Landing page + query string and Page path + query string dimensions, and appear in Page location instead.

sections.heading: Links local businesses should tag
sections.body_html:
• The website link on your Google Business Profile, for example utm_source=google, utm_medium=organic, utm_campaign=gbp.
  • Links in email newsletters.
  • Links in social media posts and bios.
  • QR codes on flyers, vehicles and signage.
  • Links in partner directories you control.

sections.heading: Google Ads uses auto-tagging
sections.body_html: Google says traffic-source data can come from manual tagging or from integrations such as Google Ads with auto-tagging. If you link Google Ads, you don't need to add UTMs to those ads.

sections.heading: Don't tag internal links
sections.body_html: Use UTMs only on links that bring people to your site from elsewhere. Tagging links between your own pages starts new attribution and muddles reports.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body_html:
• Mixing capital and lowercase letters.
  • Using different names for the same source.
  • Tagging internal links.
  • Leaving utm_medium off.
  • Forgetting to tag QR codes on print materials.

sections.heading: A simple naming sheet
sections.body_html: Create a one-page sheet that lists the exact values your business uses and share it with anyone who creates links. For example: sources such as google, facebook, instagram, newsletter, flyer and yelp; mediums such as organic, social, email, print and referral; and campaign names made of the season or offer plus the year, all in lowercase with hyphens or underscores. Add a column for the full tagged URL and the date it was created. When someone needs a new link, they copy the pattern instead of inventing names. For an Orange County business running seasonal promotions, community events and printed mailers, this simple sheet is the difference between a clean report that shows which promotion worked and a list of near-duplicate rows nobody can read.

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.body_html:
• Naming sheet created.
  • Business Profile link tagged.
  • Email links tagged.
  • Social links tagged.
  • QR codes tagged.
  • Lowercase used everywhere.

sections.heading: An example
sections.body_html: Imagine a bakery in Orange that sends a monthly newsletter, posts on Instagram and hands out flyers with a QR code. It tags each link with its own source and medium and a shared campaign name for the holiday pre-order promotion. In Traffic acquisition, the bakery sees that the newsletter brings the most pre-orders, while the flyer QR code brings few, so it changes the flyer design.

sections.heading: How this fits your local plan
sections.body_html: It helps to see where this sits in the bigger picture. Google ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and popularity, and AI assistants lean on the same public information: your Business Profile, your website, other listings and what customers write. For a business in Anaheim or anywhere in Orange County, the most reliable plan is simple and repeated: keep every listing accurate, explain each service clearly on its own page, show real proof of your work and reply to customers. Small improvements here compound, and they are far harder for competitors to copy than an ad budget.

sections.heading: What to do this week
sections.body_html:
1. Write your naming sheet.
  2. Tag your Business Profile website link.
  3. Tag your next email.
  4. Check Traffic acquisition next week.

sections.heading: When to get help
sections.body_html: Plenty of owners handle this themselves. Outside help pays off when time is short, when the business has many locations or when a problem is costing calls every day it stays unresolved. Be wary of anyone who promises guaranteed positions or asks for your verification codes or passwords; Google says nobody can pay for a better local ranking. Look for clear explanations, honest timelines and reporting tied to real enquiries. Chimera offers exactly that to businesses in Anaheim and across Orange County.

sections.heading: Where Orange County businesses lose attribution
sections.body_html: The biggest gaps we see come from links nobody thinks of as marketing. The website button on a Google Business Profile is often the busiest source of local visits, yet untagged it blends into organic search. Links in email signatures, text-message reminders, PDF quotes and invoices, printed flyers, vehicle wraps and event banners usually arrive as Direct traffic unless tagged, often through a QR code. Directory listings you control, such as Yelp or industry directories, can carry tagged links too. Go through every place your website address appears, decide which ones you can tag and add them to your naming sheet. Even tagging the five busiest sources makes reports far easier to trust, and it shows which offline marketing in Anaheim and across Orange County actually drives visits. Review the list whenever you print new materials or add a new listing, so new links are tagged from the start.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.body_html: Tag every outside link you control with utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign in lowercase, keep a naming sheet and read the results in Traffic acquisition. Chimera, based in Anaheim, sets up consistent tagging for Orange County businesses.
